issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me
issues.explanation: The negative appraisal items 'others can see what happened to me' and 'ashamed of what happened to my body' imply a trauma with visible bodily violation or injury, most classically interpersonal/sexual trauma, and are hard to reconcile with a generic man-made disaster trauma in the absence of any corroborating memory or trigger content about bodily injury or disfigurement.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Being Touched' is specifically linked to bodily violation/contact-based trauma and fits poorly with the rest of the profile for man-made disaster. The threat items center on environmental danger and escape planning, creating a cross-node mismatch with this touch-avoidance strategy.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Body Shame: I feel ashamed of what happened to my body
issues.explanation: These items imply a trauma with prominent bodily violation or physical injury consequences. For a man-made disaster trauma, this specific body-focused pattern is not impossible, but in the absence of any supporting memory or trigger content and alongside the other items emphasizing generalized danger, it stands out as a hard-to-explain shift toward an assault/injury formulation.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Being Touched: Any form of physical contact with others
issues.explanation: Within the current profile, avoidance of touch and bodily stress appears organized around bodily harm/shame, but the threat items are about environmental danger, escape planning, and unfamiliar places. That makes the strategy set only partially connected to the expressed threat/appraisal pattern.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise centered on persistent danger, vigilance, scanning, escape planning, and avoidance of unfamiliar places, which coheres with threat-focused beliefs after a man-made disaster. 'Failed Role' introduces a distinct self-evaluative theme that is not supported by the rest of the selected items and is hard to reconcile with this otherwise purely danger/safety formulation. Given the active formulation emphasizes Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies and Maladaptive Strategies → Threat, a danger-based appraisal would better fit the linked hypervigilance and checking strategies than a role-failure appraisal.

vignette: At thirty-two, Priya had spent the last six years serving on her city council, but the months following a man-made disaster at the Meridian Civic Center fractured the steady rhythm of her municipal work. Six months ago, she stood near the south staircase during a ribbon-cutting ceremony for a newly renovated public library. When the secondary power grid failed, the backup generators misfired, sending a cascade of electrical arcing through newly laid conduit. The ceiling groaned, plaster gave way, and a section of the mezzanine collapsed inward. Dust and shattering glass filled the air. Priya had been pushed toward the emergency doors by a security guard, but the crowd surging ahead of her blocked the threshold. She remembers the weight of bodies pressing against her, the sharp smell of burnt insulation, and the deafening crack as support beams snapped. The images would surface unbidden, sharp and unblinking, replaying the exact angle of the falling debris and the way the floor tilted beneath her feet. She had come to believe that the world was a dangerous place the moment the concrete gave way. In the weeks that followed, Priya found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day. Sleep became a fragmented sequence of half-awake moments where the hum of her refrigerator sounded like straining metal. She had come to believe she had to be on guard all the time, and a parallel practice emerged: she began mapping every room she entered. Before she would allow herself to sit at her desk or dine with constituents, she identified escape routes, noting which doors opened, which windows unlatched, and which corridors offered the shortest path to the street. She avoided going to unfamiliar places, certain that without the ability to assess the danger, she could not proceed. Invitations to community outreach events in newly constructed districts were declined, and medical appointments in downtown clinics were postponed until she had visited them multiple times during daylight hours to memorize the floor plans. The demands of her role as a City Council Member required her to navigate spaces that refused to yield to her planning. During a rushed site visit to a flood-damaged drainage project in the eastern ward, the ground was uneven and slick with recent rain. Situations that put her body under stress quickly surfaced as she climbed over debris and hiked up a muddy embankment, bringing on a tightness in her chest that she could not ignore. She had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next, a conviction that now sat alongside her constant vigilance. She scanned the faces of the construction crew for signs of agitation, then panned up to the load-bearing walls, then back down to the crowd. She avoided physical stress by stepping back from any situation that demanded rapid movement or elevated exertion, choosing instead to direct operations from her car parked two blocks away. When her chief of staff urged her to move toward the designated inspection path, her gaze drifted past him, locking onto structural seams and crowd density before returning to the ground. Over the months, these adaptations solidified into a rigid routine. She declined to attend the annual mayoral gala because the unfamiliar ballroom layout offered no guarantee of safe egress, a decision that quietly altered her standing among her peers. Her staff learned to anticipate her needs, arranging agenda items that kept her within the familiar boundaries of her district office, but the missed networking opportunities and delayed committee votes accumulated in quiet ways. She was certain that her role required presence, yet her attention and her body refused to comply with the pace of municipal life. What frightened her most was the realization that her own office had become a labyrinth of thresholds she could no longer cross without a mental checklist. She had finally scheduled an intake appointment after a constituent shouted during a packed town hall, causing her to bolt from the auditorium and leave her prepared remarks scattered on the floor. She sat in the therapist's waiting room today, her hands folded tightly in her lap, wondering if there was a way to attend council sessions without feeling the floor give way beneath her. She was hoping to find a way to stand in a room without scanning for exits, and she was afraid that the ground might shift again, leaving her trapped between the person she was meant to be and the body that no longer believed the world was safe.
